Think of it this way: - The Bible doesn’t mention smartphones, AI, or climate change. - It doesn’t tell you whether to accept a specific job offer or how to navigate a complex family dynamic. - It *does* teach us about love, justice, wisdom, humility, and trust in God’s character. **Those principles are meant to shape how we *approach* all situations**, even the ones it doesn’t name explicitly. > *“All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness, so that the servant of God may be thoroughly equipped for every good work.”* (2 Timothy 3:16) > Notice: it equips us for *“every good work”*— not *“every specific problem.”* The difference is crucial. Apply those principles to the context. 2. ** Seek wise counsel from your community.** - God designed us to need each其他. Proverbs 15:22 says, *“Plans fail for lack of counsel, but with many advisers they succeed.”* - Talk to mature Christians you trust. Ask: *“How would you prayerfully approach this?”* Their perspective might help you see what Scripture * implies* in this situation. 3. ** Pray for the Holy Spirit’s guidance.** - Jesus promised the Spirit would “ guide you into all truth” (John 16:13). This doesn’t mean He’ll whisper a specific answer, but He’ll sharpen your discernment over time. - Try this: *“God, I don’t have a verse for this. Help me see this through Your eyes. What would love look like here?”* 4. ** Remember: God’s grace covers your imperfect decisions.** - You’re not expected to be infallible. The Bible is full of people who made mistakes (David, Peter, Paul) but were still used by God. His grace is bigger than your uncertainty. - *“For we do not have a high priest who is unable to empathize with our weakness, but we have one who has been tempted in every way, just as we are— yet he did not sin.”* (Hebrews 4:15) 5. ** Study *how* Scripture is applied, not just * what* it says.** - Look at how Jesus handled conflicts (e.g., the woman caught in adultery in John 8), how Paul navigated cultural tensions (1 Corinthians 8), or how the early church resolved disputes (Acts 15). These show * the process* of applying biblical principles to new contexts. --- ### ** A gentle reminder: Leaning on Scripture doesn’t mean * only* leaning on Scripture.** - ** Scripture is your foundation, not your only tool.** God also gives us reason, experience, nature, and community to help us navigate life. - ** The Bible itself points us beyond itself.** Jesus said, *“I am the way and the truth and the life”* (John 14:6). He is the living Word, not just the written one. Your relationship with Him is deeper than any verse. - ** Uncertainty can be a sacred space.** When you don’t have a clear answer, it’s an opportunity to practice * trust*— to surrender control and say, *“God, I don’t know, but I trust You.”* That’s where faith grows. --- ### **Final thought:** You’re not alone in this. Even the most devoted Christians wrestle with this tension. The fact that you’re asking this question shows you’re not treating the Bible as a rigid rulebook but as a living, breathing guide to a relationship with God. **That’s exactly what He designed it to be.** - When the Bible doesn’t give a direct answer, it’s not a void—it’s a invitation to * grow* in wisdom, trust, and community. - And in those moments of uncertainty, remember: *“God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that in all things at all times, having all that you need, you will abound in every good work.”* (2 Corinthians 9:8) - He’s with you in the gray areas. You’re not alone in this. 💛

prediction.raw: **No, you are not the asshole (NTA).** Here’s why, grounded in both practical reality and ethical clarity: ### 1️️ **You had no meaningful relationship with the deceased.** - You met this "Great Aunt Wyn" **once as a toddler** (1–2 years old), when you had no capacity to form a memory or connection. - You had **never heard her name before today**. - **Funerals are for people who knew and loved the person who died**. Attending a funeral for someone you literally don’t know is not "respect"— it’s performative. Respect is shown through *genuine* connection, not forced attendance. - *Example*: If a distant cousin you’ve never met died in another country, would you feel obligated to fly across the world? No. This is the same principle. " family" doesn’t automatically mean "obligation to attend every event." ### 2️️ **Your mom’s guilt-tripping is the real issue.** - She never mentioned this great aunt to you before today, despite " supposedly playing a massive hand in raising your grandmother." If *she* didn’t even talk about this person, **why would you be expected to care?** - Her " Fine, I’ll go on my own" is emotional manipulation. **You are not responsible for her emotional needs** in this situation. - *Key insight*: If *she* had a close relationship with this great aunt, *she* should attend for *herself*— not because she’s trying to guilt you into being her emotional support. That’s not fair to you. ### 3️️ **" gatecrashing" is a valid concern.** - You’re right: **Funerals are intimate gatherings for close family and friends**. If you don’t know the person or most of the family, your presence could feel like an intrusion to * them*. - Imagine being at a funeral for someone you loved, and a distant relative you’ve never met showed up. You’d likely wonder, "Who is this person? Why are they here?" It’s not about * you* being " un family"— it’s about **context and appropriateness**. - *Real-world perspective*: In most cultures (including British), it’s understood that you only attend funerals for people you have a *personal* connection to. Distant relatives are often not expected to attend unless specifically asked. ### 4️️ **Your boundaries are healthy and necessary.** - You described yourself as " awkward at funerals for people I’ve met more than once"— that’s **self-awareness, not a flaw**. Forcing yourself into an emotionally overwhelming situation you’re not prepared for is *self-harm*, not " respect." - **Respect for yourself matters**. You don’t owe anyone a performance of grief for a person you don’t know. - *Bible connection (from our earlier conversation)*: Scripture teaches us to " love your neighbor as yourself" (Mark 12:31). ** loving yourself includes setting boundaries** when something would harm your emotional well-being. Jesus himself often withdrew to pray or rest (Mark 6:31)— He didn’t force Himself into situations He wasn’t prepared for. ### 5️️ **The " respect" argument is being misapplied.** - **True respect for the deceased is shown by those who knew them**— not by people who have no memory of them. - **True respect for your family is shown by being honest about your limits**. If you attended out of obligation, you’d likely be visibly uncomfortable or emotionally overwhelmed— which would * actually* make the funeral harder for * them*. - *Practical truth*: If the family * truly* wanted you there, they would have reached out to you * directly* (not through your mom guilt-tripping you). The fact that they didn’t speaks volumes. ### 💡 **Final verdict: NTA (Not the Asshole)** - **You are not obligated to attend a funeral for a person you’ve never known**. - **Your mom’s guilt-tripping is the problematic behavior here**— not your boundaries. - **Your self-awareness and honesty are signs of maturity, not selfishness**. > " *Do not conform to the pattern of this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind. Then you will be able to test and approve what God’s will is— his good, pleasing and perfect will.*" ( Romans 12:2) > **God’s will for you includes knowing your own limits and acting with integrity**— not performing for others’ expectations. You’re doing the right thing by honoring your own boundaries. **If you want to support your mom**: You could say, " I’m sorry I can’t attend, but I’m here for you if you need to talk about your grief. I’ll send flowers or a card to show I care." That’s * real* support— without the emotional burden of a forced attendance. 💛 *(P.S. If your mom continues guilt-tripping you, gently remind her: " I love you, but I can’t attend this funeral. I hope you understand. I’m here for you in other ways." She needs to respect your boundaries— and if she doesn’t, that’s her issue, not yours.)*
